title: The Needle and the Twenty-Four Volumes: May Morris from Red House to Kelmscott
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Red House and Queen Square, a Childhood Over the Workshops

stops.name: Red House, Bexleyheath, the birth on the Annunciation
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives 25 March 1862 at Red House, Bexleyheath, and Wikidata Q449758 carries P569 +1862-03-25. The coordinate is the one the atlas already uses for Red House in william_morris.journey.json, jane_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: The second daughter of William Morris and Jane Morris is born at Red House on the Feast of the Annunciation and christened Mary for the day. Nobody uses it. She is May from the first hour and May to the end. The house is two years old, built by Philip Webb for a marriage three years old, and it is already less a home than a workshop with beds in it. Burne-Jones and Rossetti come down from London to paint the walls, and the dining room is hung with heroines out of Chaucer that her mother and her aunt Elizabeth Burden are stitching by hand.
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath, built by Philip Webb 1859-1860, now National Trust

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the move over the workshops
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Red House is given up in autumn 1865 and the family moves to Queen Square, and the atlas pins the move at November 1865 through jane_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json. No day is recorded
stops.campa: Red House is given up and the family moves into 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury, where the Firm has taken the ground floor and the yard behind. May is three. She grows up on the floor above a business: dye vats in the yard, embroidery frames on trestles, pattern books stacked in the passage, men at work below her bedroom from morning on. Her aunt Elizabeth Burden is entered in this same house as an embroiderer. The distinction between the household and the trade is not made here, and May never learns to make it.
suggested_refs: 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury, house and workshops of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. from 1865

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the needle from her mother and her aunt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Victoria and Albert Museum states that she learned embroidery as a child from Jane Morris and Elizabeth Burden but gives no date. The year here is a placement inside her Queen Square childhood, not an attestation
stops.campa: The teaching is domestic and it is not written down. Her mother works, her aunt works, and the child is given thread and a frame and set beside them. What passes is the whole technical inheritance of the Firm's needlework: the wools, the silks, the medieval stitches the two Burden sisters recovered by unpicking old work. Bessie Burden spends her life inside this craft without an institution to her name. Her niece will hold the department, the school, the guild and the book, and begins here with the same hands over the same frame.
stops.quote: IT is only of recent years that the art of needlework has come to be divided by a hard and fast line into plain sewing and embroidery. The two branches of the art are to my mind, and indeed used to be in practice, so nearly akin that the one merges into the other, and it is surely equally desirable to teach both.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (London: Joseph Hughes & Co., 1893), Chapter I, 'Historical Glance', opening lines
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum feature on May Morris
suggested_refs: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), Internet Archive identifier decorativeneedle00morriala

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the summers on the upper Thames
stops.date_confidence: attested; the joint tenancy of Kelmscott Manor with Dante Gabriel Rossetti is taken in June 1871, the date and coordinate the atlas already carries in william_morris.journey.json, jane_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: Her father takes the Oxfordshire manor on a joint lease with Rossetti and leaves for Iceland; her mother stays at Kelmscott with Rossetti and the two girls. May is nine. What the arrangement gives her is the house: gabled limestone, a tapestry room, the Thames a field away, a summer world that is neither London nor the Firm. She is brought back to it at fifty-five to live in it, and buried a quarter of a mile from it at seventy-six. Everything between those two facts is worked out somewhere else.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott Manor, Oxfordshire, Society of Antiquaries of London

stops.name: Oneglia, the sister's seizure on the Ligurian coast
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'William Morris'; no month is given by any source consulted, and January is the atlas placement already carried in jane_morris.journey.json
stops.campa: Jane Morris takes both daughters to the Ligurian coast. At Oneglia, Jenny suffers a severe epileptic seizure, and William Morris crosses Europe at speed to reach them. May is thirteen and watches the family divide itself permanently into the sister who is ill and the sister who is not. Jenny is cared for the rest of her life, fifty-nine more years of it. May does the caring, the earning, the editing and the keeping of the name, and no source records anyone asking her whether she wanted the arrangement.
suggested_refs: Oneglia, now part of Imperia, Liguria; the Morris family's Italian journey of 1876

stops.name: Venice, the tour that continues anyway
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year only; Wikipedia 'William Morris' names Venice, Padua and Verona as stops on the 1876 journey without dates, and April is the atlas placement carried from jane_morris.journey.json
stops.campa: The crisis passes and the family goes on being tourists. Venice, then Padua, then Verona, the cities her father invokes all his working life when he wants to say what craft looked like before machines. The record of this leg comes from his biography and not from hers. No letter of May's from these weeks has surfaced, and what a girl of fourteen made of the mosaics her father had been lecturing about since before she was born is not on paper anywhere that has been found.
suggested_refs: Venice, Padua and Verona, named stops of the Morris family journey of 1876

segments.name: The School and the Upper Mall

stops.name: National Art Training School, South Kensington, the government school
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through the Victoria and Albert Museum's feature on May Morris; no month is recorded and January is the atlas default. The coordinate is the South Kensington Museum site on which the school stood
stops.campa: At sixteen she enrolls at the National Art Training School on the South Kensington Museum site, the government school that becomes the Royal College of Art. It is the first instruction she receives that is not her mother's or her aunt's. The museum next door holds the historic needlework of Europe in cases, and she will measure modern work against it for the rest of her life. Formal drawing and design go on top of twelve years spent in the workshops, and seven years after she enrolls she is running a commercial department.
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum feature on May Morris
suggested_refs: The National Art Training School, South Kensington, forerunner of the Royal College of Art

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, the move to the Upper Mall
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'Kelmscott House' gives the family in residence from October 1878, the date and coordinate the atlas already carries in william_morris.journey.json and jane_morris.journey.json. No day is recorded
stops.campa: The family takes the Georgian house on the Upper Mall and her father renames it Kelmscott House for the manor upriver. May is sixteen. This becomes the fixed address of her adult life. The coach house behind it will be a socialist lecture hall, the room upstairs will hold her invalid sister, the printing office two doors along will be the Kelmscott Press, and her father will die in this house eighteen years from now. The Thames outside runs to Kelmscott, and he likes to say so to anyone who will listen.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott House, 26 Upper Mall, Hammersmith, home of the Morris family from October 1878

stops.name: Merton Abbey Works, the vats on the Wandle
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the works; Morris relocates the dyeworks from Queen Square to Merton Abbey in June 1881, the date and coordinate the atlas carries in william_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json. The often repeated claim that May began work for the firm at Merton Abbey in 1880 is impossible on those grounds, and the 1880 start year itself is unsupported by any source retrieved
stops.campa: The Firm moves its dyeing and weaving out of Bloomsbury to seven acres on the river Wandle at Merton: madder and indigo vats sunk into the floor, tapestry looms upstairs, water clean enough to wash the wools in. May is nineteen and the work she does for the house is not yet a post with a name. Between the Merton sheds and the Oxford Street showroom the embroidery trade is divided in some way, and how it was divided in these years is not documented in anything reachable.
suggested_refs: The Merton Abbey Works on the river Wandle, occupied by Morris & Co. from June 1881

stops.name: 449 Oxford Street, director of embroidery at twenty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'May Morris' ('aged 23') and Wikipedia 'Morris & Co.' ('in 1885, when she was in her early twenties'); no month is recorded and January is the atlas default. The coordinate is 449 Oxford Street near the Marble Arch end and is approximate
stops.campa: At twenty-three she is made director of the embroidery department of Morris & Co. The post is new only in being named. Her mother and her aunt built the practice by hand in a dining room at Bexleyheath and a house in Queen Square, without title, wage scale or catalogue entry between them. May inherits the whole of it and runs it as a business: designs, kits sold to be worked at home, commissions, a workroom of women paid for their hours. She holds the department eleven years, until her father dies.
stops.quote: True talent, like true genius, is never slovenly; for the acquiring of this quality of order and care, on which I lay so much stress, is part of the apprenticeship that every worker with hand and eye must go through, be it in workshop or studio, or labouring alone and self-taught, towards excellence in any art.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), chapter on workmanship
suggested_refs: Morris & Co. showroom, 449 Oxford Street, London

stops.name: The coach house at Kelmscott House, the Socialist League Sundays
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Hammersmith branch of the Socialist League and its Sunday meetings in the coach house, which the atlas dates to February 1885 in william_morris.journey.json. May Morris's own attendance is not separately documented in the sources consulted and is reconstruction from the household
stops.campa: Behind the house the coach house is fitted out as a lecture hall for the Hammersmith branch of the Socialist League. Sunday evenings bring speakers and audiences through a building her family lives in. Bernard Shaw is a regular. Henry Halliday Sparling is the League's secretary. The man she will marry and the man she will not are both in the room, and she is twenty-three, runs a department, and is a socialist in her own right. Her father is the one remembered speaking in this coach house. The record of her own presence in it is thinner, though the room is the same room she grew up over.
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott House coach house, meeting hall of the Hammersmith Socialist Society

stops.name: London, the Valentine sent to Shaw
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a Guardian piece of 2017 reports Shaw noting a Valentine in his diary on 14 February 1886, reached in this session only through a search summary and not through the diary itself. The place is generic London, not a documented address
stops.campa: She paints a Valentine by hand and sends it to Bernard Shaw. He records it in his diary in four words and does not name her. What passes between the two of them over the next fifty years is contested by everyone who has written about it: an understanding she believed in, a mystic betrothal he described later in his own terms, a marriage she makes to another man in the League while the question is open. The card is one of the very few pieces of it that carries a date.
stops.quote_source: George Bernard Shaw, diary entry for 14 February 1886, as reported in The Guardian (2017)
sources: Sally Peters, 'From Mystic Betrothal to Menage a Trois: Bernard Shaw and May Morris' (JSTOR), via search summary
suggested_refs: Bernard Shaw's diaries for 1886, ed. Stanley Weintraub

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, Bloody Sunday
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the event and the date, which the atlas carries in william_morris.journey.json. May Morris's presence in the square is not attested in any source consulted and is reconstruction from the household's politics
stops.campa: Police and two regiments clear a demonstration out of Trafalgar Square. Her father is in it. Alfred Linnell dies of what is done to the crowd, and Morris writes the death song for his funeral. May is twenty-five, a paid officer of a decorating firm that sells to the rich and a member of a household that spends its Sundays arguing for the abolition of the arrangement. Both halves of that are hers. She never resolves them, because the Firm is also the only place the work she cares about gets made.
suggested_refs: Bloody Sunday, Trafalgar Square, 13 November 1887, and the funeral of Alfred Linnell

stops.name: The New Gallery, Regent Street, the exhibitions that name the movement
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society and its use of the New Gallery from 1888, the coordinate the atlas carries in elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json. The particular showings in which May Morris's work hung are not itemized in the sources consulted, and January is the atlas default
stops.campa: The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society takes the New Gallery on Regent Street and gives the movement the words it will be called by. Her embroidery hangs there among her father's textiles and Burne-Jones's designs, and so does her aunt's, catalogued under a name of her own for the first time in that room. The Society exhibits craftswomen and prints their names. The Art Workers' Guild, which supplies most of the exhibitors, will not admit them, and May Morris is nineteen years from doing anything about it.
suggested_refs: The New Gallery, 121 Regent Street, and the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society catalogues from 1888

stops.name: Fulham Register Office, the marriage to Sparling
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the wedding; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives 14 June 1890 at Fulham Register Office, the date and coordinate the atlas carries in jane_morris.journey.json. The duration is contradictory across the record: jane_morris.journey.json says the marriage lasts under five years, while the divorce is given as 1898. Not resolved here
stops.campa: She marries Henry Halliday Sparling, secretary of the Socialist League, in a register office and not a church, which is the family's politics showing. She is twenty-eight and running the embroidery works. Her mother married at nineteen a man she did not love and stayed fifty-five years. The daughter marries at twenty-eight for what looks like love and is out of it inside a decade. Sparling stays in the orbit of the Kelmscott Press. Shaw goes on being in the room, and everyone who writes about the marriage says so.
suggested_refs: Marriage entry of May Morris and Henry Halliday Sparling, Fulham, June 1890

stops.name: The Kelmscott Press, Hammersmith, the father's last workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Kelmscott Press is founded in January 1891, the date and coordinate the atlas carries in william_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: Two doors from the family house her father sets up a press to make the ideal book: his own type, his own paper, his own ink, and Edward Burne-Jones drawing the woodcuts. May is twenty-nine, married, and living inside the project's radius. The Press runs seven years and prints fifty-three titles. Twenty years from now she will edit twenty-four volumes of his writing for a commercial publisher in London, which is the same labour done by other means, with her name on the introductions and his on the spine.
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott Press at 14 and 16 Upper Mall, Hammersmith, 1891-1898

stops.name: London, Decorative Needlework goes to press
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives Decorative Needlework (Joseph Hughes & Co., 1893) and OpenLibrary confirms first publication in 1893. No month is recorded, and the place is the publisher's London rather than a documented address
stops.campa: Joseph Hughes and Company publish her manual. It is written by the working head of a commercial department and not by a collector, and it says so: history in the first chapter, stitches and materials in the middle, design and its abuses at the end, and throughout an insistence that the student go to the Middle Ages for a standard because the present has none. She is thirty-one. It becomes the technical reference for two generations of English embroiderers, and it is the first book with her name alone on the title page.
stops.quote: THESE pages are written for and dedicated to those who, without much previous knowledge of the art of embroidery, have a love for it and a wish to devote a little time and patience to its practice.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (London: Joseph Hughes & Co., 1893), Dedicatory Note, opening lines
suggested_refs: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (London: Joseph Hughes & Co., 1893)

stops.name: South Kensington Museum, the old work behind the book
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source retrieved states that May Morris researched Decorative Needlework in the South Kensington collections. The link is drawn from the book's historical chapters and from her training on the site, and the date is arbitrary within the year of publication
stops.campa: The museum she trained beside holds the historic needlework of Europe in cases, and the book's argument runs on it: that modern embroidery does not compare well with the work of any earlier period, and that the fault lies in design and not in skill. She is not an antiquarian making a case for the past. She is a manufacturer telling her own trade that it is worse than it used to be, and she keeps the standard where students can walk to it rather than inside a theory.
stops.quote: It is here, to the Middle Ages, I repeat, the student must go for example and inspiration towards serious work: modern embroidery does not compare favourably with that of any period, but it is the very antithesis to the early art, and it is indeed time that something was done to raise it to a higher level.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), Chapter I, 'Historical Glance'
sources: Victoria and Albert Museum feature on May Morris
suggested_refs: The textile and embroidery collections of the South Kensington Museum, now the Victoria and Albert Museum

segments.name: The Father's Death and the Teaching Circuit

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, William Morris dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; 3 October 1896 at Kelmscott House, the date and coordinate the atlas already carries in william_morris.journey.json, jane_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: He dies in the house on the Upper Mall at sixty-two, of being William Morris, as one of his doctors puts it. May is thirty-four. She inherits, jointly with her mother and her sister, the manor, the papers, the reputation and the unfinished business of a man who wrote poetry, ran a factory, founded a press and spent his last thirteen years arguing for revolution. From this month her own designing gives way to the administration of his estate. She never fully gets it back: the manor, the papers, and the twenty-four volumes still to come will occupy the rest of her working life.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, where William Morris died on 3 October 1896

stops.name: Kelmscott churchyard, the tomb by Philip Webb
stops.date_confidence: attested; the burial at St George's, Kelmscott, under a tomb designed by Philip Webb, the date and coordinate the atlas carries in william_morris.journey.json and jane_morris.journey.json
stops.campa: He is carried from the station on a hay wain and buried in the village churchyard under a ridge-roofed stone that Philip Webb designs, the architect who built the house she was born in. May is chief mourner at thirty-four. Her mother will be buried here in eighteen years, her sister in thirty-nine, and she herself in forty-two, four graves in one ground within sight of the manor. The circuit that closes at this gate opens at Red House, and Webb draws both ends of it.
suggested_refs: The tomb of William Morris, St George's churchyard, Kelmscott, designed by Philip Webb

stops.name: Regent Street, the Central School of Arts and Crafts
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives her teaching embroidery at the LCC Central School from 1897. The school is founded in 1896 in Morley Hall, rented from the Regent Street Polytechnic, and does not move to Southampton Row until 1908, so the Southampton Row address commonly attached to this date is anachronistic. The coordinate is the Regent Street Polytechnic building and is approximate; no source retrieved gives Morley Hall's exact address
stops.campa: The London County Council's new school takes rented rooms off Regent Street and she begins teaching embroidery in them. She is thirty-five. What passed to her in a Bloomsbury sitting room from two women who were never paid for teaching it now goes to enrolled students in a municipal classroom, on a timetable, with a syllabus. She becomes head of the embroidery department in 1899, holds it six years, and stays on as Visitor until 1910. Thirteen years of her working life go into a municipal classroom instead of a workroom.
stops.quote: Having said this much, I must here say what I mean by design worthy to be wedded to good work.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), chapter on design
sources: Wikipedia, 'Central School of Art and Design'
suggested_refs: The LCC Central School of Arts and Crafts, founded 1896, first housed in Morley Hall at the Regent Street Polytechnic

stops.name: London, the divorce and the name taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'May Morris'; no month is recorded and the place is generic London. The atlas's jane_morris.journey.json describes the marriage as lasting under five years, which does not fit a 1890 wedding and an 1898 divorce; the discrepancy is left open
stops.campa: The marriage to Sparling ends and she goes back to being Morris. She is thirty-six, without a husband, without a father, with an invalid sister, a mother in her sixties, a house in Hammersmith, a manor in Oxfordshire and the literary estate of the most famous decorator in England. She keeps the name because it is the name of the estate she is now administering, and because Shaw, who is the reason given by everyone who writes about the marriage, does not marry her either.
suggested_refs: Divorce record of May Morris and Henry Halliday Sparling, 1898

stops.name: Birmingham School of Art, the circuit out of London
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date; Wikipedia 'May Morris' names Birmingham, Leicester and Hammersmith as places where she taught but gives no years. 1900 is a placement inside her documented teaching decade of 1897 to 1910
stops.campa: She teaches embroidery in Birmingham, in a city with an Arts and Crafts culture strong enough to have grown its own. The Birmingham school produced the illustrators of the Kelmscott Press's later books; her father's press and her father's circle reached this place before her. She teaches method: the order of a stitch, the choice of a thread, the point at which work is checked against old work. Her students will never see the Merton workroom where she learned to do that checking, so she carries the standard up to them.
stops.quote: The deduction from this is, therefore, not to draw a line you do not understand and cannot explain to yourself. Be definite before everything — let every form you put on paper be something, explain something.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), Chapter VII, 'Design, Convention and Realism'
suggested_refs: The Birmingham School of Art, Margaret Street, and its Arts and Crafts teaching

stops.name: Leicester School of Art, the Hawthorn Building
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the source names the city only, not the school, the syllabus or the years. The coordinate is the Hawthorn Building on The Newarke, which housed the Leicester School of Art, and the date is a placement inside her teaching decade
stops.campa: Leicester is a name in a list. The source that records her teaching here records nothing else: not what she taught, not how often, not who sat in the room. The same gap runs through most of the evidence about her working life. Her father's lecture tours are printed, dated and reprinted. Hers survive as three city names inside a single sentence, and the students who learned a stitch from her in the Midlands are not recorded at all, by name or by number.
stops.quote: In the later work — and I am careful to speak of late Renaissance, as the early style has a beauty and delicacy all its own — we have the convention which has forgotten all about nature, or thinks to improve upon it, spinning ideas out of itself like a silkworm.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), Chapter VII, 'Design, Convention and Realism'
suggested_refs: The Hawthorn Building, The Newarke, Leicester, former home of the Leicester School of Art

stops.name: Hammersmith School of Art, the loop closed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date; Wikipedia 'May Morris' names Hammersmith among the schools where she taught without giving years, and 1903 is a placement inside her documented teaching decade
stops.campa: The third school is a walk from the house she grew up in. She teaches in the district where the Socialist League met in her family's coach house, where the Press printed, and where her father died. The whole of her working geography can be covered on foot in an afternoon: Upper Mall to the school, the school to the river, the river upstream to Kelmscott. Three schools, one department, one guild and a manual in print, all of it inside a few square miles of west London. She leaves that ground once, for five months, and crosses the Atlantic to do it.
suggested_refs: The Hammersmith School of Arts and Crafts, Lime Grove

stops.name: Bloomsbury, the Women's Guild of Arts founded
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the founders through Wikipedia 'May Morris'; no month is recorded. The coordinate marks the Bloomsbury district of the Art Workers' Guild rather than a documented meeting address for the Women's Guild
stops.campa: The Art Workers' Guild, which is the professional body of everyone she works among, will not have women in it. She founds the Women's Guild of Arts with Mary Elizabeth Turner, joined by Mary Annie Sloane, Ethel Fanny Everett, Mabel Esplin and Letty Graham, and it becomes the leading association for craftswomen in England. She is forty-five and has run a department for twenty-two years without being eligible for the club her male colleagues belong to. She does not petition the Guild. She starts a second one and admits the women it will not.
suggested_refs: Records of the Women's Guild of Arts, founded 1907

stops.name: Southampton Row, the school gets a building
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the school's move to purpose-built premises in Southampton Row in 1908 (Wikipedia, 'Central School of Art and Design'); whether May Morris taught in the new building during her remaining Visitor years to 1910 is not stated by any source consulted. No month is recorded
stops.campa: The Central School moves into a purpose-built block on Southampton Row, put up to teach the crafts as crafts. She is no longer head of embroidery; she has been Visitor since 1905 and remains one two years more. The department that began in rented rooms off Regent Street now has workshops, kilns and a permanent address on a London street. Twelve years after her father's death the crafts he lectured about are taught out of the rates by the London County Council, and in embroidery the person who put them on the timetable is his daughter.
stops.quote: To my thinking, satin-stitch is rather clumsy when worked with thick silk or wool.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), chapter on stitches and technique
sources: Wikipedia, 'Central School of Art and Design'
suggested_refs: The Central School of Arts and Crafts building, Southampton Row, opened 1908

stops.name: The Port of New York, landing for the lecture tour
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the month; the Textile Society of America paper 'The Reluctant Reformer: May Morris' United States Lecture Tour of 1909-1910' gives an October 1909 arrival in New York. The exact day, the ship and the pier are not named, and the coordinate is the Manhattan waterfront
stops.campa: She lands in New York at forty-seven to lecture for five months on embroidery and the Arts and Crafts movement. It is the longest journey of her life and the only extended one she makes without her family around her. America wants the Morris name and gets a working designer with opinions about what women are paid. Within days she is at suffrage and labour meetings in the city. The scholarly title given the tour afterwards calls her a reluctant reformer, which is the American reading of what happened rather than hers.
sources: Textile Society of America, 'The Reluctant Reformer: May Morris' United States Lecture Tour of 1909-1910' (digitalcommons.unl.edu)
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests for the port of New York, October 1909

stops.name: Hull House, Chicago, a month at the settlement
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the stay and roughly its length; the Textile Society of America paper and the Jane Addams Hull-House Museum both record about a month based at Hull House during the tour. The precise dates are not given and November is a placement
stops.campa: She spends about a month based at Hull House on Halsted Street, Jane Addams's settlement on the Near West Side, lecturing across Chicago from an address in the middle of the country's most famous experiment in urban reform. An English designer of independent means could have taken a hotel. She takes a room in a house full of immigrant families, labour organisers and a craft workshop run on the argument her father made in a Hammersmith coach house: that how a thing is made is a political question.
sources: Jane Addams Hull-House Museum blog, 'The Hidden Legacy of May Morris'
Textile Society of America, 'The Reluctant Reformer'
suggested_refs: Hull House, 800 South Halsted Street, Chicago

stops.name: Glessner House, Prairie Avenue, the lecture on design in costume
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the lecture and the venue through the Glessner House archive blog; the exact date within the Chicago stay is not recorded, and 15 November is a placement inside it
stops.campa: She lectures on design in costume to Frances Glessner's Monday Morning Reading Class in a Richardson house on Prairie Avenue papered throughout with Morris and Company goods. The guestroom carries Arcadia, which May designed. She is explaining design to a room of wealthy Chicago women from inside her own pattern, hired by a customer who already bought it. Two miles west, Hull House runs a craft workshop for people who cannot. She sleeps at the second address and lectures at the first.
stops.quote: For work done at the demand of fashion or caprice and that done inevitably, that is, for its own sake, are as widely dissimilar as can be: the first being discarded in a month or so as ridiculous and out of date, and the other remaining with us in all its dignity of beauty and fitness, to be guarded as long as may be against the unavoidable wear and tear of time.
stops.quote_source: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), Dedicatory Note, closing paragraph
suggested_refs: Glessner House, 1800 South Prairie Avenue, Chicago, and the Arcadia wallpaper in its guestroom

stops.name: Detroit Museum of Art, the handicraft societies
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; an Archives of American Art item records a Detroit lecture for the Detroit Society of Arts and Crafts, but the citation could not be re-fetched in this session and no date within the tour is given. The coordinate is the museum's Jefferson Avenue building, which it occupied from 1888 until 1927
stops.campa: The Detroit Society of Arts and Crafts brings her to the museum on Jefferson Avenue. The American handicraft guilds are the movement's second generation, founded on her father's books and lectures, and they receive her as an inheritance made flesh. What arrives instead is a lecturer who keeps turning the subject to who does the work and what the work pays, in a country where the craft revival is largely a matter of prosperous women's afternoons. She has run a workroom and met a payroll, which none of her hosts has done.
sources: Archives of American Art (aaa.si.edu), item 'May Morris', not re-fetchable in this session
suggested_refs: Records of the Detroit Society of Arts and Crafts, founded 1906

stops.name: The North Atlantic, the crossing home
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the return in March 1910 follows from the tour's stated five-month duration and its October 1909 start. No source consulted names the ship, the port of departure or the port of arrival, and the coordinate is a mid-ocean placeholder rather than a position
stops.campa: Five months end and she goes home. Nothing about the voyage is on record: no vessel, no dates, no port. The pin is a point in open water chosen to mark a passage that certainly happened and was certainly written down somewhere nobody has found. She is forty-eight, and the designing half of her life is behind her. What waits at the far end of the crossing is twenty-four volumes of her father's prose and the rest of her life spent inside them, in London and then in a house on the upper Thames.
sources: Inference from Textile Society of America, 'The Reluctant Reformer'; no direct source for the return voyage found
suggested_refs: Transatlantic passenger lists, spring 1910

stops.name: London, the Collected Works begun
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'May Morris'; the Collected Works of William Morris is issued by Longmans, Green and Company between 1910 and 1915. No month is recorded and June is arbitrary within the first year
stops.campa: Longmans, Green and Company begin issuing the Collected Works of William Morris, edited by his daughter, with her introductions in front of each volume. She is forty-eight. The job runs five years and comes to twenty-four volumes: the poems, the romances, the lectures, the translations, the socialist journalism, arranged and annotated by the only person alive who watched the whole of it being written. Her own designing effectively stops. The standard edition of her father's work is the largest thing she ever makes.
suggested_refs: The Collected Works of William Morris, ed. May Morris, 24 vols (London: Longmans, Green, 1910-1915)

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the freehold bought
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Wikipedia 'Kelmscott Manor' records Jane Morris purchasing the freehold in 1913, and Wikipedia 'Jane Morris' adds that she bought it a few months before her death to secure it for her daughters. No month is given. The claim, repeated in some summaries, that May took up residence in 1913 is unsupported by any source retrieved; her documented residence begins in 1917
stops.campa: Her mother buys the manor outright after forty-two years of leasing it, and does it explicitly to secure the house for two unmarried daughters, one of them permanently ill. Jane Morris does not go back to live in it. May is fifty-one and still in London with the volumes. The house that has been a summer place since she was nine becomes property, and the property is a provision for a future in which neither daughter has a husband and one of them cannot be left alone in a room.
suggested_refs: Conveyance of the Kelmscott Manor freehold to Jane Morris, 1913

stops.name: 5 Brock Street, Bath, Jane Morris dies
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and place through the atlas's jane_morris.journey.json, which pins the death at 5 Brock Street, Bath, on 26 January 1914. The research pool flagged this as drawn from standard biography rather than from a source re-fetched in this session
stops.campa: Her mother dies at Bath a few months after buying the manor, aged seventy-four, and is buried at Kelmscott beside her husband. May is fifty-one and now head of the family: one sister who cannot manage her own affairs, two houses, an estate and a reputation with her father's name on it and her handwriting all through it. Of the four people who lived at Red House when she was born, two are in the churchyard at Kelmscott and one is being cared for. She is the one still standing.
suggested_refs: 5 Brock Street, Bath, where Jane Morris died on 26 January 1914

stops.name: London, the twenty-four volumes finished
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year of completion through Wikipedia 'May Morris'; no month is recorded and the place is the publisher's London
stops.campa: The last volume goes out in the second year of the war. She is fifty-three. The introductions she wrote for the set are the first sustained account of William Morris by somebody who lived in the house with him, and they become a primary source for every biographer who follows. Her name stands on them as editor. For most of the century afterwards the sentence written about her begins with the word daughter, and these twenty-four volumes are the reason it does.
suggested_refs: May Morris's introductions to the Collected Works, reissued as Introductions to the Collected Works of William Morris (1973)

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, Mary Lobb comes to the house
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'May Morris', which dates her living at Kelmscott with Mary Lobb from 1917; no month is recorded. This is the earliest dated anchor for May Morris's residence at the manor, which is why the 1913 residence claim is rejected above
stops.campa: She settles at the manor with Mary Lobb, a Women's Land Army volunteer who comes to work the fields and stays twenty-one years. They live together until May dies. The sources call Lobb a companion and go no further, and no letter, deposition or diary consulted here settles what the word covered. What is documented is the arrangement itself: two women, one house, two decades, a village that gets used to them, and two cottages built in the village in her father's vernacular manner.
suggested_refs: The memorial cottages at Kelmscott village, commissioned by May Morris

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the sister dies and the house is hers
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year through Wikipedia 'Kelmscott Manor', which places Jenny Morris's death immediately before May's outright inheritance of the house; no month is recorded and January is the atlas default
stops.campa: Jenny dies at seventy-four, having been ill since a seizure on the Ligurian coast fifty-nine years earlier, and the manor passes to May alone. She is seventy-three. The care ends after fifty-nine years. It set the terms of the earning and the editing and of keeping two houses running at once, and now nothing depends on it. What is left is a house full of her father's furniture, a mother and a father and now a sister in the churchyard up the lane, and a decision to make about who is to have all of it when she is gone.
suggested_refs: Jane Alice 'Jenny' Morris, 1861-1935, buried at St George's, Kelmscott

stops.name: Oxford, William Morris: Artist, Writer, Socialist
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the two-volume study is commonly cited as published by Basil Blackwell at Oxford in 1936, but this session's fetches did not confirm publisher, place or date directly. The coordinate is Blackwell's on Broad Street and is approximate
stops.campa: The two volumes come out as a companion to the Collected Works: her father's life and his politics, written at seventy-four out of family papers nobody else has seen. It is the last of the editorial labour and the only part of it that is unmistakably authorship. Biographers use it for the next ninety years as a primary source, which is to say they mine it for him rather than read it as hers. She is both the witness and the writer, and the catalogue files her under his name.
sources: General art-historical reference; not independently verified in this session
suggested_refs: May Morris, William Morris: Artist, Writer, Socialist, 2 vols (Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1936)

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the letter to Shaw
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the sentence is quoted from Sally Peters' study of Shaw and May Morris, reached in this session only through a search summary. The source dates it late in her life without a precise year or month, and 1936 is a placement, not an attestation. The place follows her residence, not a documented letterhead
stops.campa: She writes to Bernard Shaw, fifty years after the Valentine, and tells him what nobody else told her. He is famous, honoured by every institution that matters, and has spent decades being amusing in print about the Morris household. She is a designer whose patterns were sold under her father's name, an editor whose introductions are quoted without her, and the founder of a guild for the women the men's guild would not have. The sentence is not a complaint. It is a correction filed late against a record she knew was wrong.
stops.quote: I'm a remarkable woman, always was, though none of you seemed to think so.
stops.quote_source: May Morris to George Bernard Shaw, late in her life, cited in Sally Peters, 'From Mystic Betrothal to Menage a Trois: Bernard Shaw and May Morris'
suggested_refs: The Shaw-May Morris correspondence, British Library and the Shaw papers

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'May Morris' and Wikidata Q449758 (P570) both give 17 October 1938 at Kelmscott Manor, aged seventy-six, which is consistent with the birth date of 25 March 1862
stops.campa: She dies in the manor at seventy-six, in the house she first saw at nine from the far side of a summer, in a building her father took on a joint lease with the painter who was in love with her mother. Mary Lobb is in the house. The village is a quarter of a mile off. Everything she administered for forty-two years, the estate, the papers, the furniture, the reputation and the argument about who made what, is under this roof and now has to go somewhere.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott Manor, Oxfordshire, where May Morris died on 17 October 1938

stops.name: St George's churchyard, Kelmscott, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the place; Wikidata Q449758 records her place of burial as St George's Churchyard, Kelmscott (Q114737519), and the coordinate is the one the atlas already carries for her father and mother. The day of the funeral is not recorded in any source consulted, and 20 October is a placement
stops.campa: She is buried at St George's, in the ground that holds her father under Philip Webb's ridged stone, her mother beside him and her sister with them. Four graves in one churchyard, a quarter of a mile from the house, at the end of a family that began in a stable yard in Holywell and a boy's bedroom in Walthamstow. Her father was carried here on a hay wain in 1896 and the village turned out for him. What is written down about her own funeral is the fact of the grave.
suggested_refs: St George's churchyard, Kelmscott, Oxfordshire, Wikidata Q114737519

segments.name: The House She Kept, After Her

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the bequest Oxford declines
stops.date_confidence: attested as to both ends; Wikipedia 'Kelmscott Manor' records the 1938 bequest to Oxford University on condition the contents be preserved, and the transfer to the Society of Antiquaries of London in 1962 when the University found the arrangement unworkable. No month is recorded for the transfer
stops.campa: She leaves the manor and everything in it to Oxford University, on condition that the contents stay together and the public be let in. The University tries it for twenty-four years and hands the whole thing to the Society of Antiquaries of London, which holds it still. Her aunt Elizabeth Burden's embroidered St Catherine from the Red House scheme is in that collection. The house reopens in 2022 after six million pounds of restoration and takes some twenty-six thousand visitors a year through rooms she arranged.
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott Manor collection, Society of Antiquaries of London

stops.name: The William Morris Gallery, Walthamstow, her own name on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year; Anna Mason and others, May Morris: Arts and Crafts Designer (Thames and Hudson, 2017), is published alongside a William Morris Gallery exhibition of the same name, and Jan Marsh publishes 'Feminist, socialist, embroiderer: the untold story of May Morris' in the same year. The opening date was not confirmed in this session and October is a placement
stops.campa: Seventy-nine years after her death, the gallery in her father's boyhood house hangs her work under her own name and a book goes out with it. Designs sold for decades as his are given back to her. The same gallery has put a label on her aunt Elizabeth Burden. A further exhibition at the Lady Lever Art Gallery is reported for 2026 on a single source that could not be checked against a second. The recovery has taken seventy-nine years, which is longer than the working life it recovers.
sources: Anna Mason et al., May Morris: Arts & Crafts Designer (2017)
suggested_refs: The William Morris Gallery, Lloyd Park, Walthamstow
